corrected_proposal.title: Trump Says U.S. Strikes Hit Three Iranian Nuclear Sites in Truth Social Post
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump’s June 21 Truth Social post said U.S. forces had attacked three Iranian nuclear sites and called for peace.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: An archive of Donald Trump’s June 21, 2025 Truth Social posts records a message saying the United States had completed an attack on three Iranian nuclear sites and naming Fordow, Natanz and Esfahan. He wrote, “NOW IS THE TIME FOR PEACE!” The archived post does not contain the supplied title’s phrase “MISSION ACCOMPLISHED IRAN!” This correction records Trump’s published words without treating his success claim as an independent damage assessment.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On June 21, 2025, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the United States had completed an attack on three Iranian nuclear sites. The archived post names Fordow, Natanz and Esfahan, says the aircraft had left Iranian airspace, and calls for peace. This is the wording preserved in the American Presidency Project’s dated archive of Trump’s Truth Social posts. The supplied record’s title attributed the phrase “MISSION ACCOMPLISHED IRAN!” to him, but that wording does not appear in the June 21 post reviewed here. The corrected copy therefore describes the contemporaneous message without putting that phrase in Trump’s mouth. Trump characterized the military operation as successful; the post does not independently establish the amount of damage or the status of Iran’s nuclear program. PolitiFact’s subsequent review quoted military experts saying it was too soon to know whether the sites had been completely destroyed. The event captured here is Trump’s public announcement and its stated call for peace, not a finding about the operation’s effectiveness or the later course of the conflict.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump’s Foreign Aid Freeze Disrupts Gaza Assistance Despite Exemptions
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump’s Foreign Aid Freeze Disrupts Gaza Assistance Despite Exemptions
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid while programs were reviewed. Reuters reported that exemptions included $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza, while the Associated Press later reported that hundreds of millions in USAID payments to aid groups remained frozen and officials had no confirmed payments to Middle East partners. The evidence supports disruption, not a complete cutoff of all Palestinian aid.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid while the administration reviewed whether programs aligned with its foreign-policy priorities. Reuters reported that the pause halted funding across assistance programs and later reviewed a list of exemptions, finding that only limited humanitarian relief was released. Among the approved exceptions were $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza. That limited carveout makes the frozen entry’s claim that all U.S. aid to Palestinians was eliminated inaccurate. The interruption still had reported effects: in March, the Associated Press reported that hundreds of millions of dollars in USAID contractual payments to aid groups were frozen, and that officials had no confirmed payments to partners in the Middle East after the January 31 Gaza waiver. The reporting distinguishes authorization from delivery: more than $383 million was approved for Gaza relief, while payment remained unconfirmed. The supported event is therefore a broad aid freeze that disrupted Gaza assistance despite exceptions, not a completed categorical cutoff of every Palestinian program. The cited reports do not establish the frozen entry’s annual aid total, a Foreign Assistance Act violation, or a specific administration rationale about Palestinians.

WASHINGTON, Feb 21 (Reuters) - The Trump administration released $5.3 billion in previously frozen foreign aid, mostly for security and counternarcotics programs, according to a list of exemptions reviewed by Reuters that included only limited humanitarian relief.

President Donald Trump ordered a 90-day pause on foreign aid shortly after taking office on January 20, halting funding for everything from programs that fight starvation and deadly diseases to providing shelters for millions of displaced people across the globe.

In contrast to security-related programs, USAID programs received less than $100 million in exemptions, according to the list. Exempted USAID programs included $78 million for non-food humanitarian assistance in Gaza, which has been devastated by war.

The Trump administration’s cuts to USAID have frozen hundreds of millions of dollars in contractual payments to aid groups, leaving them paying out of pocket to preserve a fragile ceasefire, according to officials from the U.S. humanitarian agency.

USAID was supposed to fund much of the aid to Gaza as the ceasefire progressed, and the Trump administration approved over $383 million on Jan. 31 to that end, according to three USAID officials. But since then, there have been no confirmed payments to any partners in the Middle East, they said.

corrected_proposal.description_long: An earlier Trump Files record says Donald Trump claimed at an April 2024 campaign event that he had beaten Barack Obama in the 2016 presidential election, then repeated the error in the same context. That entry identifies Hillary Clinton as Trump’s 2016 opponent and says Obama was not on the ballot. The alleged remark would confuse the person Trump defeated with a former president who was not his opponent. The supplied record gives no date beyond the month, venue, transcript, or recording, so it does not establish the exact wording or that the remark was repeated. This draft preserves the claim as supplied for internal review; it does not present it as a verified quotation. The original record also asserted significant media scrutiny and comparisons with Joe Biden, but supplied no supporting source for that reaction, so those claims are omitted. Its inference about cognitive dysfunction is also omitted because the packet does not document experts making that assessment about this incident. Keep this card unpublished unless a source identifies the April event and establishes its wording and context.
